name: Motivated tactician
statement: The motivated tactician is a framework rather than an effect: it holds that people pick among thinking strategies according to their goals, so only its particular predictions can be tested.
meaning: Fiske and Taylor describe five successive pictures of the social thinker: consistency seeker, naive scientist, cognitive miser, motivated tactician and activated actor. Their fourth edition dates the motivated tactician to the 1990s and glosses it as a fully engaged thinker with several cognitive strategies available, who chooses among them, consciously or not, on goals, motives and needs. The claim is about strategy selection, not about a direction of error. It predicts that the same perceiver will sometimes take a shortcut and sometimes think hard, and that a goal manipulation will move which one happens. Nothing in it says whether the resulting judgement will be too harsh, too generous or too confident. Its concrete form is the continuum model of impression formation, in which perceivers start from a category and move towards attribute-based impressions when category fit is poor or motivation is high. That model, and not the label, is what carries testable content.

origin.who: Susan T. Fiske and Shelley E. Taylor
origin.note: Fiske's own curriculum vitae lists Fiske, S. T., & Taylor, S. E. (1991), Social cognition (2nd ed.), New York: McGraw-Hill, the edition the term is normally placed in. No copy of that edition was opened for this entry, and no source read here shows the phrase inside it. The Internet Archive holds two scans of it, both under controlled lending, and both answer this session with an item-not-available notice rather than a paywall. What was read is the authors' fourth edition, which says the 1990s view of the social perceiver 'might best be termed the motivated tactician', and their 2020 retrospective, which makes the Motivated Tactician the second of four phases after the Cognitive Miser. Both trace the slogan that thinking is for doing to William James, and cite Fiske's 1992 Journal of Personality and Social Psychology centennial article for it, the fourth edition adding her 1993 paper alongside. That article is closed at the publisher and was checked only against its Crossref record, which confirms the volume, issue and pages.

evidence: The framework's evidence is the evidence for its members. Neuberg and Fiske ran three experiments in which participants expected to interact with a young man formerly hospitalised as a schizophrenic. In the first, short-term task-oriented outcome dependency led participants to base impressions on the man's particular attributes rather than on the label, and to spend more time attending to those attributes. The second showed that the attention effect was not merely a matter of impression positivity. The third manipulated an accuracy goal instead and produced the same shift. The paper's abstract, which is what is open, reports no effect sizes. Fiske and Neuberg then set out the continuum model across 74 pages of Advances in Experimental Social Psychology. Fiske and Taylor's own account of the second wave is that it addressed replicability by identifying moderator variables, primarily goals and motivations; their abstract names interdependence and threat, and the body of the same essay adds power. Three things complicate that account. Kunda and Thagard report two sets of meta-analyses inside a theory paper. Studies of individuating information average r = .71, against r = .25 for stereotypes in the absence of individuating information, and across the 40 studies that varied both orthogonally the averages are r = .69 and r = .19, which the authors restate as 48% of the variance in target evaluations against 4%. They argue that a parallel constraint-satisfaction network needing little conscious inference reproduces most impression-formation findings. Reynolds and Oakes manipulated interdependence in one experiment and accuracy goals in another, and read their results as showing that whether the salient self-other categorisation is interpersonal or group-based explains variability in impression formation. Carpenter ran a series of meta-analyses of the elaboration likelihood model's argument quality by processing type predictions, k = 134, and reports the data as generally consistent with the predicted interaction.

replication.headline: No replication of the motivated tactician was located, because there is no motivated-tactician experiment to repeat. The tested claims sit one level down, and they disagree.
replication.detail: Searches for a direct or conceptual replication of Neuberg and Fiske's outcome-dependency experiments, and for a meta-analysis of the continuum model's motivational moderators, returned neither on 21 September 2026. What exists is a set of neighbouring results. Kunda and Thagard use their meta-analyses to argue that the serial architecture the continuum model assumes is not needed to fit the findings, while granting that parallel integration is compatible with that model and was raised by its authors. The first pair of meta-analyses prints no study count. The later one, which sets the two kinds of information against each other in the same designs, rests on 28 articles reporting 40 studies. Lerner and Tetlock reviewed the accountability literature, the most studied motivational moderator of effort, and organised it around the question of when accountability attenuates, does not affect, or amplifies cognitive biases, which is a moderator that runs in three directions. Vrantsidis and Cunningham then tested continuum-model predictions directly, in seven studies built on a Bayesian account of when a category is overused. Six found no evidence that occupation categories are overused at all, and none under cognitive load or information consistency, though the authors report some doubt about whether the load manipulation worked. The seventh found overuse where background goals made the category relevant and processing resources were limited, which is the shape of answer the framework predicts. From an adjacent literature outside person perception, a preregistered direct replication tested whether a goal manipulation shifts processing at scale. Roozenbeek, Freeman and van der Linden re-ran Pennycook and colleagues' accuracy nudge for COVID-19 headlines. Their first stage, n = 701, was unsuccessful at p = .67. After a second round, pooled N = 1,583, the treatment by discernment interaction reached uncorrected p = .017, with truth discernment at d = 0.14 in the treatment group and d = 0.10 in the control group, against d = 0.14 and d = 0.05 in the original. The goal manipulation survived and its advantage over the control condition shrank by about half.

limits: The framework does not forbid an outcome. A perceiver who takes a shortcut is a motivated tactician conserving effort, and a perceiver who individuates is a motivated tactician pursuing accuracy, so a single study cannot go against the label, only against a named moderator. That is the cost of the design Fiske and Taylor describe as a response to replicability, and it is why this page maps members rather than issuing a verdict. The search covered Crossref bibliographic queries for replications and meta-analyses of the continuum model and of outcome-dependency impression formation, PubMed, Europe PMC, the Internet Archive and general web search, on 21 September 2026, and turned up follow-on, neuroimaging and modelling work rather than replication attempts. Several documents stayed shut. The 1991 second edition of Social Cognition is held at the Internet Archive only as restricted lending scans. Fiske's 1992 article and Fiske and Neuberg's 1990 chapter are closed at their publishers and were checked against their Crossref records, ScienceDirect answering with a bot challenge rather than a paywall notice. Reynolds and Oakes was read as its Crossref abstract, which does not say how large their interdependence and accuracy-goal effects were; the Australian National University's repository holds the file but releases it only through a request-a-copy form. Vrantsidis and Cunningham was read as the publisher's abstract for the version published in September 2026, not as the 2025 preprint, and the two were not compared. The accuracy-nudge replication concerns news sharing, not impression formation, and is quoted here as evidence about goal manipulations in general. Entry 464 covers the elaboration likelihood model, where Carpenter's meta-analysis is weighed at length.
misreadings: Calling it a bias is the first error. It names a model of the perceiver, it predicts no systematic departure from any norm, and a list of cognitive biases is the wrong place to look for it. The second error is treating it as a refutation of the cognitive miser. Fiske and Taylor keep the miser as one setting of the tactician, writing that people are sometimes cognitive misers and sometimes deeper thinkers depending on their purpose. The third is misattributing the miser itself: their fourth edition credits the cognitive miser model to S. E. Taylor's 1981 work, while their own 2020 retrospective ties the Cognitive Miser phase to their 1984 book. A fourth error is reading Fiske and Taylor's claim that the approach addressed replicability as a demonstration that it did. Their claim is that specifying goals and motives as moderators makes findings conditional and therefore reproducible, and the accountability literature shows the same moderator producing attenuation, no effect and amplification. Neuberg and Fiske's experiments are also read too widely. They show that outcome dependency and accuracy goals push attention towards a target's attributes in a laboratory task built around a psychiatric label, which is not the same as showing that wanting to be fair defeats a stereotype.

sources.text: Fiske, S. T., & Taylor, S. E. (2021). Social cognition: From brains to culture (4th ed.), Chapter 1. SAGE. Read as the publisher's free sample chapter, which carries the five models of the social thinker and Table 1.1. The publisher answered 403 on re-check in September 2026, and the file was read from the Wayback Machine's replay of it.

Fiske, S. T., & Taylor, S. E. (2020). Social Cognition evolves: Illustrations from our work on Intergroup Bias and on Healthy Adaptation. Psicothema, 32(3), 291-297. Read in full as the journal's own open PDF. Crossref records the volume and issue the other way round.

Neuberg, S. L., & Fiske, S. T. (1987). Motivational influences on impression formation: Outcome dependency, accuracy-driven attention, and individuating processes. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 53(3), 431-444. Read as its abstract at PubMed, which carries the design and the direction of all three experiments and no effect size. The full text is closed at the publisher.

Read as a scan with no text layer, whose 25 pages, 284 to 308, were recovered page by page by optical character recognition.
